texts.facts: The appellants have averred that on 26.06.2018, Ms. Jiji Marry Johnson, Food Safety Officer (FSO), took sample of "Besan (Tata Sampann)" from Sh. Arun Goyal, FBO-cum-Proprietor of M/s Goyal Store, 101-A, Sarojani Park, Shastri Nagar, Delhi - 110031, for analysis under the Food Safety & Standards Act, 2006 and after analysis, declared the said sample to be misbranded vide report dated 06.07.2018, opining that the declaration "Low Oil Absorb Besan" is misleading and likely to create erroneous impression regarding its character and same is in violation of Regulation No. 2.2.1.3 read with 2.3.1.5 of the Food Safety & Standards (Packaging & Labeling) Regulations 2011. Notice of the appeal was sent to the Food Safety Officer, record of the Adjudicating Officer was also called for. A perusal of the above shows that a raid was conducted by the Food Safety Pitamber Pitamber Dutt Dutt Date: 2026.02.12 18:14:21 +0530 Arun Goyal & Ors Vs State (Through FSO FSAT) Page no. 5 of 12 Officer on 26.06.2018 and sample of Besan (Tata Sampann) was taken, which was declared to be misbranded vide report dated 06.07.2018, therefore, a complaint was submitted by the FSO against the appellant for violating provisions of Section 23 (1), Section 26 (1) & 26 (2) (ii), Section 27 (1) and Section 27 (2) (c) Read with Section 3 (1) (zf) (A) (a) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and violated Regulation no. 2.2.1.3 Read with 2.3.1.5 of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging & Labelling) Regulations, 2011, punishable under Section 52 (1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. 7. Pursuant to the said complaint, notice was sent to the appellants, who submitted their detailed reply. 9. The appellants have claimed that the impugned order dated 03.10.2023 is not sustainable in law as same has been passed in a very cryptic manner, without assigning any reason. A perusal of the material shows that appellants challenged the complaint filed by Food Safety Officer on various grounds, which they have taken in their reply. As per the appellants, while taking a sample for analysis, the officer concerned was bound to give notice in writing to all the respondents for analysis of sampled commodity to an accredited laboratory as per Section 47 (1) (c) (iii) of the FSS Act. The complainant Pitamber Pitamber Dutt Dutt Date: 2026.02.12 18:14:30 +0530 Arun Goyal & Ors Vs State (Through FSO FSAT) Page no. 6 of 12 however, failed to do so, therefore, violated the mandatory provision of Section 47 of the Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006. 11. The appellants have further claimed that the complaint filed by the respondent was barred by limitation as per Section 77 of the FSS Act, 2006, because the reason vide which extension was granted, were not placed on record.
texts.arguments: 4. Sh. Saurabh Awasthi, Ld. Counsel for the appellants has contended that the impugned order has been passed by the A.O. / ADM in a mechanical manner, without appreciating and distinguishing the submissions / objections and the documents so relied by the appellants in their reply / objections. He further contended that the complaint was barred by limitation, under Section 77 of the FSS Act, 2006 and the extension of time so granted by the concerned Commissioner, Food Safety was not a valid extension and suffered from infirmity. He further contended that the statement "Low Absorb Besan" was the characteristic of the product and further the report analysis was based on pick and choose method by isolating the said declaration from the other statement made on the label. He further contended that the A.O. / ADM has failed to appreciate the order of Advertising Standard Council of India (ASCI) dated 17.03.2016 under FSS Act, placed by the appellants before it, wherein a similar complaint was disposed of in favour of appellant no. 8 Tata Chemicals. He further contended that the report of the Food Analyst was vague and ambiguous, without any contra-material to show that how the statement "Low Absorb Besan" was misleading / misbranded. He further averred that no notice under Section 46 (4) of FSS Act dated 11.07.2018 was ever sent or delivered to appellants no. 5 to 8. He further contended that A.O. / ADM, while passing the impugned order has failed to appreciate that appellants no. 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 were entitled for Arun Goyal vs State, Through Fso on 12 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/2326668/ 3 benefit of guarantee and due-diligence as per provisions of Section 26 (4) and 80 (B) (2) of the Food Safety & Standards Act, 2006 as they were neither the manufacturer nor the packer / labeler of the sampled commodity and had Pitamber by Pitamber Dutt Dutt Date: 2026.02.12 FSAT no. 16/2023 18:13:56 +0530 Arun Goyal & Ors Vs State (Through FSO FSAT) Page no. 4 of 12 sold / supplied / purchased the said commodity in original sealed condition against valid invoice / bill. He further contended that the Food Analyst Laboratory, Delhi was not recognized by the Food Authority and accredited by NABL at the relevant time. He further contended that the sanction granted under Section 36 (3) (e) of the FSS Act, 2006 by the Designated Officer was granted in a routine and mechanical manner. He further contended that no independent witnesses were engaged at the time of sampling. He further contended that the appellants herein were deprived of their right to cross-examine the witness in spite of objections to this effect. He prayed that appeal may be allowed and impugned order dated 03.10.2023 may be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. 5. Sh. Birender Singh Dagar, Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor for the State / FSO has contended that the the impugned order has been passed by the FSO after considering the reply filed by the appellants and material available on record, as per law. He further contended that the sample taken was opined to be of misbranded by the Food Analyst vide his report no. FSS/1063/2018 dated 06.07.2018, being in violation of Regulation no. 2.2.1.3 read with 2.3.1.5 of the Food Safety & Standards (Packaging & Labelling) Regulation, 2011. He further contended that copy of Food Analyst Report was sent to FBO and other concerned, pursuant to which respondents no. 3 to 8 appeared through their counsel and filed their written reply and after considering the Food Analyst Report, reply and submissions made by both the parties, the FSO has passed a well reasoned order. He prayed that appeal may be dismissed. 14. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in "M/s Kranti Asso. Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. Vs Masood Ahmed Khan & Ors.", Civil Appeal, arising out Pitamber Digitally signed by Pitamber Dutt Dutt Date: 2026.02.12 18:14:39 +0530 Arun Goyal & Ors Vs State (Through FSO FSAT) Page no. 7 of 12 of SLP (Civil) no. 20428 of 2007, date of decision 08.09.2010 , after analyzing various judgments on necessity of giving reason by a body or Authority in support of his judgment, summarized various pleas and observed in para 51, as under:- 51. Summarizing the above discussion, this Court holds: a. In India the judicial trend has always been to record reasons, even in administrative decisions, if such decisions affect anyone prejudicially. b. A quasi-judicial authority must record reasons in support of its conclusions. Arun Goyal vs State, Through Fso on 12 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/2326668/ 5 c. Insistence on recording of reasons is meant to serve the wider principle of justice that justice must not only be done it must also appear to be done as well. d. Recording of reasons also operates as a valid restraint on any possible arbitrary exercise of judicial and quasi-judicial or even administrative power. e. Reasons reassure that discretion has been exercised by the decision maker on relevant grounds and by disregarding extraneous considerations. f. Reasons have virtually become as indispensable a component of a decision making process as observing principles of natural justice by judicial, quasi-judicial and even by administrative bodies. Pitamber by Pitamber Dutt Dutt h. The ongoing judicial trend in all countries committed to rule of law and constitutional governance is in favour of reasoned decisions based on relevant facts. This is virtually the life blood of judicial decision making justifying the principle that reason is the soul of justice. i. Judicial or even quasi- judicial opinions these days can be as different as the judges and authorities who deliver them. This is important for sustaining the litigants' faith in the justice delivery system. k. If a Judge or a quasi-judicial authority is not candid enough about his/her decision making process then it is impossible to know whether the person deciding is faithful to the doctrine of precedent or to principles of incrementalism. l. Reasons in support of decisions must be cogent, clear and succinct. It cannot be doubted that transparency is the sine qua non of restraint on abuse of judicial powers. Transparency in decision making not only makes the judges and decision makers less prone to errors but also makes them subject to broader scrutiny. (See Arun Goyal vs State, Through Fso on 12 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/2326668/ 6 David Shapiro in Defence of Judicial Candor (1987) 100 Harward Law Review 731-737). n. Since the requirement to record reasons emanates from the broad doctrine of fairness in decision making, the said requirement is now virtually a component of human rights and was considered part of Strasbourg Jurisprudence. See (1994) 19 EHRR 553, at 562 para 29 and Anya vs. University of Oxford, 2001 EWCA Civ 405, wherein the Court referred to Article 6 of European Convention of Human Rights which requires, "adequate and intelligent reasons must be given for judicial decisions". o. In all common law jurisdictions judgments play a vital role in setting up precedents for the future. Therefore, for development of law, requirement of giving reasons for the decision is of the essence and is virtually a part of "Due Process". 15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in case titled Jaspal Singh Jolly Vs Municipal Corporation of Delhi, reported as 125 (2005) DLT 592, has held that:- "Noting the decision of the Supreme Court as Erusia Digitally signed Pitamber by Pitamber Dutt Dutt Date: 2026.02.12 18:15:07 +0530 Arun Goyal & Ors Vs State (Through FSO FSAT) Page no. 10 of 12 Equipments & Chemical Ltd. Vs State of West Bengal, (1975) 1 SCC 70: AIR 1975 SC 266 (at P. 269); 106 (2003) DLT 573, Mekaster Trading Corporation Vs Union of India; and (1990) 4 SCC 594, S.N. Mukherjee Vs Union of India, I had held that the aforesaid decision established the legal proposition that orders which are subject to judicial review must be in compliance with the principle of natural justice, namely (a) proper hearing, (b) decision by an unbiased mind; (c) taking into consideration all the relevant factors and excluding the irrelevant factors; and (d) reasons to be recorded.
